Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A small red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with the low sun and its golden path on the water and a purple hill on the far shore.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

10 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The red sailboat with its white sails, right of center (hull about 69% to 86% across, 57% to 63% down), set against the orange sky and its reflection below it. Light: The setting sun, low in the sky just left of center (48% across, 42% down). It lights the sky gold around it, throws a golden path down the water toward the viewer, and catches the left edges of the sails.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: laying in and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: dabbing the sun diskRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: the hill and the shoreline bandFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #4 round: the small bright dashes near the shorelineRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the mast and boomLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

STEP 1 OF 10

Paint the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and just left of center, so every highlight in this painting faces it.
  2. Sky violet across the top 10% with the 1 inch flat, long side-to-side strokes, creamy paint.
  3. Coral pink from 10% to 20% down, blending the join with the violet while wet.
  4. Sunset orange from 20% down to just past halfway (about 55%), a little below where the shoreline will go.
  5. Golden glow worked into the orange in the middle, 30% to 45% down, around where the sun will sit. Let the sky dry.
Paints for this step4 paints, 4 new
  • Sky violet new3 parts ultramarine, 3 parts white, 1 part red
  • Coral pink new3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine
  • Sunset orange new3 parts red, 3 parts white, 1 part yellow
  • Golden glow new4 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 2 parts red

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat side to side across the whole width, then stroke back over each join while it's wet so the bands melt into each other.

Watch out: Wipe the brush on a paper towel before going from orange back into violet, or it turns muddy brown.

Watch out: Colors dry a little darker, so test each mix on the palette edge first.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: After the redo the sky still stops at about 54% down, not 58%, so sun and hill also show white canvas right under the shoreline band. Paint what the steps say.

Heads up, this picture is a little off: Spotted after round 2: the third sky render still stops at 53.7% down, so the picture shows the sky ending right at the shoreline. The redo cap for the step is used up. The step text tells the painter to run the orange to about 55%, a little past where the shoreline will go. Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 10

Paint the sun

  1. Let the sky dry first.
  2. Sun yellow in a circle centered 48% across and 42% down, about 0.7 inch wide, dabbed with the #8 round.
  3. Two or three thin coats, drying between, so no orange shows through.
  4. Dab a little golden glow around the edge to soften it.
Paints for this step2 paints, 1 new
  • Sun yellow new6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red
  • Golden glow from step 1, mix more if it has dried4 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 2 parts red

Brushes

#8 round

Strokes

Dabbing. Tap the round's tip straight down, turning it slightly each time, to build a solid circle with a soft edge.

Watch out: A light color over orange needs 2 to 3 thin coats; one thick coat goes streaky.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 10

Paint the far hill and shore

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. Hill purple with the 1/2 inch flat, strokes following the slope: top at 12% across, 40% down; left side off the canvas at 43% down; slope ending at 47% across, 50% down.
  3. Shoreline navy in a level band across the full width, 50% to 54% down, flat on its side.
  4. A pale far ridge on the right: hill purple mixed into coral pink, nearly dry, scrubbed from 55% across to the edge, top 46% down, bumping up to 40% at 75% to 85% across.
Paints for this step3 paints, 2 new
  • Hill purple new3 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of red
  • Shoreline navy new1 part ultramarine, a touch of yellow, a touch of white
  • Coral pink from step 1, mix more if it has dried3 parts white, 2 parts red, 1 part ultramarine

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Pull the flat along the hill's slope, from the top down to the right, so the hill reads as one sloped shape.

Horizontal strokes for flat ground. Keep the flat level and the strokes long for the shoreline band.

Scumbling. Wipe the flat nearly dry and scrub it lightly in small sideways strokes so the ridge stays hazy and the orange shows through.

Watch out: Keep the shoreline level: measure 50% and 54% down at both edges and connect them.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 10

Paint the teal water

  1. Mid teal with the 1 inch flat just under the shoreline, long level strokes across the full width.
  2. Deep teal from about 65% down to the bottom edge, blending the join into the mid teal while wet.
  3. Leave a few streaks of each teal showing rather than blending it flat. No white canvas should show anywhere now.
  4. Let the water dry.
Paints for this step2 paints, 2 new
  • Mid teal new3 parts ultramarine, 2 parts white, 1 part yellow
  • Deep teal new3 parts ultramarine, 1 part yellow, 1 part white

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat side to side across the whole width; stroke back over the join between the two teals while wet.

Watch out: Keep every stroke level, or the water looks tilted.

Watch out: The picture shows faint lighter and darker patches going up and down in the water; ignore them and keep your streaks level.

The raw render was clean. Paint what the steps say.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 10

Paint the sun's path on the water

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. A thin line of path gold right under the shoreline, 23% to 66% across, with the flat's edge.
  3. Below it, rows of two to four short level dashes down to about 95%: path gold in the middle, sunset orange at the ends, teal gaps between, as in the diagram.
  4. Rows sit at 33% to 55% across near the top and widen to 25% to 66% around 75% to 88% down. The left quarter stays teal.
  5. A few small sun yellow dashes in the middle near the shoreline with the #4 round.
Paints for this step3 paints, 1 new
  • Path gold new3 parts yellow, 2 parts red, 2 parts white
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried3 parts red, 3 parts white, 1 part yellow
  • Sun yellow from step 2, mix more if it has dried6 parts white, 3 parts yellow, 1 part red

Brushes

1/2 inch flat#4 round

Strokes

Horizontal dashes on water. Touch the flat's edge down and pull it sideways a short way, lightly loaded. Short and close together near the shoreline, longer and farther apart lower down.

Watch out: Leave teal between the dashes; a solid gold stripe won't look like water.

Watch out: This is the ugly stage for many painters. That's normal; keep going.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 10

Paint the red hull

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. Build the hull with Hull red as in the diagram, using the #8 round: it spans 72% to 93% across, its top edge at about 58% down and its bottom at 63%.
  3. Fill it with strokes along its length. Two coats so no teal shows through.

Brushes

#8 round

Strokes

Building from pieces. Draw the top line first, then the curved bottom up to the point, and fill between them.

Watch out: Keep the top edge nearly level; a tilted hull looks like it's sinking.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 10

Paint the white sails

  1. Let the hull dry.
  2. Mark the mast line lightly: straight up at 81% across, from the hull to 27% down.
  3. Sail white for the left triangle with the 1/2 inch flat: from the tip down to the hull, its base from 73% to 81% across at 57% down. Stroke down from the tip.
  4. The right triangle the same way, its base from 81% to 90% across.
  5. Two or three thin coats so no orange shows through.

Building from pieces. One triangle at a time, each from the shared mast line, so the two meet in a straight vertical edge.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 10

Add the mast, boom, and boat shading

  1. Let the sails dry.
  2. Mast brown, thinned like ink, with the liner: a straight line at 81% across from 26% down to the hull, then the boom along the right sail's bottom to 90% across.
  3. Mid teal in a thin strip between the sails' bottom edge and the hull, 73% to 90% across, so the water shows under the sails.
  4. Dark red along the bottom of the hull with the #4 round, then a thin sail white rim along its top edge.
  5. Sail shadow, nearly dry: a soft blue-gray band down the left sail beside the mast, and one diagonal fold across the right sail.

Brushes

Liner (#1 or #0)#4 round

Strokes

Liner work. Hold the liner upright and pull the mast in one steady stroke, top to bottom, with light pressure.

Dry brush. Wipe the round nearly clean and drag it lightly down the sails so the fold lines stay soft and broken.

Watch out: Reload the liner often or the mast line skips.

Watch out: Try a liner line and a dry-brush stroke on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 9 OF 10

Paint the boat's reflection

  1. Let the water dry.
  2. Dark red pulled straight down under the hull with a nearly dry 1/2 inch flat, 64% to 68% down, 72% to 93% across. Once dry, pull two or three thin level lines of mid teal across it.
  3. Reflection white in short level dashes below it, down to about 92%: wide at the top (73% to 90% across), narrowing to 79% to 84% at the bottom, teal between them.
  4. Let the dashes dry. Then mast brown in a zigzag straight down at 81% across with the liner, to about 94%.

Brushes

1/2 inch flatLiner (#1 or #0)

Strokes

Vertical pull-down. Wipe the flat nearly dry and stroke straight down from the hull's waterline for a soft, streaky red.

Zigzag. Wiggle the liner side to side as you pull down, small and even, so the mast looks bent by the ripples.

Watch out: Keep the reflection softer and more broken than the boat, or it looks like a second boat.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Numbers are steps. A dashed, struck-through number was tried on that rung first and didn't hold up. Claude starts at the top and pays for a render only when nothing free will do.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A red sailboat on teal water at sunset, with the sun, its path on the water, and a purple hill.

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: The image is the painting edge to edge, with no screen, frame, page, or border around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape

Done: crop

Left out: about 7.5% from each side: the left end of the hill and empty water and shore on the right

Why: The picture is wider than an 11 x 14 canvas turned sideways. The boat, its reflection, the sun, and its path all fit inside a crop, so no extend render was needed.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things besides the boat, which is the subject. No textures of hundreds of items: the sky streaks and water ripples are one repeated stroke each. No fine detail inside big shapes. About eight parts (sky, sun, hill, shoreline, water, sun path, boat, reflection), within the budget of 8 for a 154 sq in canvas.

Changed: nothing dropped or merged

Why: The picture is already a simple, loose painting a beginner could follow.

A calm sunset seascape: a violet-to-orange sky, a low sun just left of center, a purple hill on the far left, teal water with the sun's golden path, and a small red sailboat with white sails and a zigzag reflection on the right. What matters is the warm-cool contrast (orange sky, teal water) and a clean, simple boat. The hard parts for a beginner are keeping the shoreline level, laying light sails over orange, and making the sun path and reflection read as water with broken dashes instead of solid stripes.

Subject: A small red sailboat with white sails on calm teal water at sunset, with the low sun and its golden path on the water and a purple hill on the far shore.
Focal point: The red sailboat with its white sails, right of center (hull about 69% to 86% across, 57% to 63% down), set against the orange sky and its reflection below it.
Light: The setting sun, low in the sky just left of center (48% across, 42% down). It lights the sky gold around it, throws a golden path down the water toward the viewer, and catches the left edges of the sails.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sunset sky gradient (violet top, coral pink, orange, gold glow near the sun)
  2. the sun
  3. the far hill and the dark shoreline band
  4. the teal water
  5. the sun's golden path on the water
  6. the red hull
  7. the white sails
  8. mast, boom, hull rim and shadows
  9. the boat's reflection
  10. light ripple dashes and sparkles on the water
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

The photo is a classic YouTube-style paint-along scene: a sky gradient, far shapes, water, then one simple subject and its reflection, all back to front on white canvas. That is exactly the paint-along technique, and its water-reflection rules (sun path in horizontal dashes, reflection pulled down, zigzag mast) fit this picture.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

It starts with toning, sketching, and a flat block-in, which the owner's paint-alongs skip, and its fixed stages would add steps (tone, sketch) that this simple scene doesn't need.

How the paint recipes were worked out17 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order10 steps

Back to front: the sky first (run a little past the horizon), then the sun on the dry sky, then the far hill and shoreline over the sky, then the water, then the sun's path on the dry water (reflections go after what they reflect). The boat goes on next, built as the hull, then the sails, then the thin details (mast, boom, rim, shading), and only then its reflection, since a reflection is painted after the object is done. A last step adds the few far glints the finish shows on the left water.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky

    The farthest thing, and every later layer sits on it, so it goes first and runs past the horizon.

  2. 2. Paint the sun

    A light disk over orange needs its own dry base and two or three coats, so it gets its own small step.

  3. 3. Paint the far hill and shore

    The far hill and shoreline sit in front of the sky and behind the water; the shoreline sets the horizon everything else lines up with.

  4. 4. Paint the teal water

    The water covers the bottom half and must be dry before the sun path and reflections go on it.

  5. 5. Paint the sun's path on the water

    The sun's reflection goes on once the water is dry, and before the boat so the boat sits on top of a finished sea.

  6. 6. Paint the red hull

    The main subject's biggest piece first; the sails stand on it.

  7. 7. Paint the white sails

    The sails stand on the hull and sit over the sky, so they come after both; light over dark needs the sky dry.

  8. 8. Add the mast, boom, and boat shading

    Thin lines (mast, boom, rim) and shading go on dry paint last, as the teacher's details step for the subject.

  9. 9. Paint the boat's reflection

    A reflection is painted after the object it reflects, directly under it, softer and broken.

  10. 10. Last glints on the water

    The finish has a few far gold glints on the left water that no earlier step paints; they are the last small marks.

Filters it tried9 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams3 steps, free

Three steps needed a picture of how to build them: the sun path (rows of dashes that widen), the hull, and the sails. The rest are fills, gradients, a circle, or thin lines whose place the words give in grid numbers.

  • Step 5: Paint the sun's path on the water beginner check (step review proposal)

    Noticed: The step review found that a dozen rows of dashes with nothing showing how one row is built left the painter guessing, and the words needed more than a sentence for how the rows widen.

    Pieces: A thin gold line under the shore first, then short rows of two dashes near the top, then wider rows of four with orange at the ends lower down: the order a painter lays them.

  • Step 6: Paint the red hull beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object appears whole in one step; a beginner needs to know where to start the hull's outline.

    Pieces: The top edge as one nearly level line, then a shallow curve under it rising to the pointed bow on the right, then fill along its length. That's how a boat is drawn: deck line first, then the belly.

  • Step 7: Paint the white sails beginner check

    Noticed: Two shaped pieces that must meet on one straight line; without a guide line the sails come out lopsided or overlapping.

    Pieces: A light mast line first, then the left triangle from it, then the right one, a little wider, as in the picture (8% versus 9% of the canvas width).

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A gradient of horizontal bands; the bands and their heights are in the words.
  • Step 2: A circle with its center and size given.
  • Step 3: One simple slope; the top, left edge, and end of the slope are given as grid positions.
  • Step 4: A flat fill in two teals with level strokes.
  • Step 8: Straight lines (mast, boom, rim) and a few soft shadows on shapes already painted; positions are in the words.
  • Step 9: The picture shows the three layers plainly and each instruction gives its position and size; a diagram would repeat the picture.
  • Step 10: Three short dashes with their positions given.

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check The water came out a bright blue-cyan instead of the photo's green teal.
  • Finish check The hill came out a stronger blue-violet than the photo's soft muted purple.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The image model kept stopping the sky at the horizon even when told twice to run it to 58% down; three renders all ended at about 54%. The words now carry it, but a sky step might work better with a filter that extends the finish's sky downward.
  • lock-steps' backward pass left faint vertical light and dark patches in the water (where the sun path and the reflection go later) and a faint warm patch in the sky step where the sails go. The raw renders were clean; the tone shift toward the finish seems to bring in the finish's broad tone around those features.
  • The finish showed a teal strip between the sails and the hull that the sails step didn't; the details step carries it as an instruction. Planning the sails' bottom edge a little above the hull would have matched the finish.
  • The plan's last step planned light teal ripples and sparkles that the finish doesn't really show; the step review caught it. Plan the last step from what the finish adds, measured against the step before, not from what such scenes usually have.
  • Stroke choices for a sailboat (outline the hull, then the sails as two triangles from a mast line) aren't in the research notes; they come from general drawing practice.
